question: What are the two core behavioral areas used to understand autism?

options.A: Aggressive outbursts and profound sleepiness
options.B: Social communication challenges and repetitive behaviors
options.C: Hyperactivity and attention deficits
options.D: Memory loss and sudden physical paralysis

explanation: Spot on! Autism is primarily identified by differences in how a person communicates socially, alongside a preference for repetitive routines or movements.

question: Why is it so tricky to make drugs that kill parasites without harming human patients?

options.A: Parasites share a similar eukaryotic cell structure with human hosts
options.B: Human immune systems cannot produce antibodies against parasites
options.C: Parasites replicate much faster than bacterial pathogens
options.D: Antiparasitic medications are always destroyed by stomach acid

explanation: You've got this! Because both human cells and parasites are eukaryotic (complex cells with a nucleus), it's tough to design a medicine that attacks the parasite without hurting our own cells.

question: A skull pin accidentally slips out while a patient is in traction. What is your very first emergency action?

options.A: Run out of the room to find the primary doctor
options.B: Remove the remaining pins with a bedside wrench
options.C: Add more weights to the traction rope system
options.D: Manually support the head in a neutral position

explanation: Don't panic! Hold the patient's head steady with your hands first to keep the neck safe, then call for help.

question: Why do nurse researchers rely so much on a theoretical framework?

options.A: It connects abstract nursing ideas directly to concrete patient care
options.B: It replaces the literature review section of the proposal
options.C: It guarantees that the research will be published in a journal
options.D: It eliminates the need for statistical data analysis entirely

explanation: Nursing is all about practice! Frameworks help us bridge the gap between big academic ideas and the real-world care we give patients every day.

question: Where do Clostridium tetani spores normally live before getting into the body?

options.A: Within fresh breast milk
options.B: Inside clean tap water supplies
options.C: On healthy human skin surfaces
options.D: In soil, dust, and animal feces

explanation: Correct! These tough spores hang out in soil, dust, and animal waste, just waiting for an opening to enter the body.

question: Why is taking leftover antibiotics a bad idea when you catch a common cold?

options.A: Colds require heavy surgical intervention instead of drug therapy
options.B: Cold viruses are already completely immune to all human medicines
options.C: Antibiotics change into sweet syrups when exposed to cold air
options.D: Colds are caused by viruses, whereas antibiotics only target bacteria

explanation: Remember: antibiotics fight bacteria, not viruses. Taking them for a viral cold does zero good and only helps build resistance.

question: Why do patients with Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) end up bleeding severely?

options.A: Blood pressure drops so low that blood can no longer flow through vessels
options.B: The bone marrow completely stops making red blood cells and white cells
options.C: The liver starts destroying all circulating proteins in the blood plasma
options.D: All available platelets and clotting factors are used up by widespread tiny clots

explanation: DIC is a confusing condition where the body goes into overdrive, forming tiny clots everywhere. This uses up all the clotting resources, leaving none behind when a real bleed happens elsewhere.

question: What is the key difference between monitoring and evaluation?

options.A: Monitoring is done only by doctors, while evaluation is done strictly by patients
options.B: Monitoring happens after the project closes, while evaluation happens before it starts
options.C: Monitoring looks at financial costs, whereas evaluation only looks at weather patterns
options.D: Monitoring is ongoing during the project, while evaluation is a formal assessment of results

explanation: Monitoring is continuous tracking to keep things on track, while evaluation measures the final outcomes and impact. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T15#GNS225_U2_T15_h7)

question: Why is building a trusting relationship important during continuing care?

options.A: It legally binds the patient to live at the clinic
options.B: It keeps the patient engaged and compliant with their treatment plan
options.C: it stops family members from getting involved in care
options.D: It allows the nurse to avoid documenting patient interactions

explanation: Trust makes patients feel safe sharing their true feelings and concerns, which helps prevent them from dropping out of care. [learn more](GNS314_U4_T5#GNS314_U4_T5_h3)

question: What three categories are evaluated using the Glasgow Coma Scale?

options.A: Heart rate, breathing rate, and blood pressure
options.B: Eye opening, verbal response, and motor response
options.C: Reflex speed, muscle tone, and pain tolerance
options.D: Cranial nerve integrity, balance, and coordination

explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale measures these three specific behavioral responses to quantify a patient's level of consciousness. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T1#GNS222_U3_T1_h8)

question: Which piece of information is most critical to document immediately during a patient's admission assessment?

options.A: Known drug allergies
options.B: Favorite television programs
options.C: Previous occupation history
options.D: Preferred clothing brand

explanation: Documenting allergies immediately prevents the accidental administration of medications that could cause severe or life-threatening reactions. [learn more](GNS112_U2_T5#GNS112_U2_T5_h3)

question: What happens when an osteoblast gets completely trapped inside the hard bone it built?

options.A: It divides rapidly to form new osteons
options.B: It transforms back into a stem cell
options.C: It dissolves into the central canal
options.D: It turns into a mature osteocyte

explanation: Spot on! Once it's completely surrounded by the hard matrix, the builder cell settles down into a maintenance worker known as an osteocyte.

question: What is the main reason we use computers and digital tools in clinical nursing?

options.A: To make healthcare delivery safer and more efficient
options.B: To reduce the number of registered nurses needed in a hospital
options.C: To eliminate all verbal communication among healthcare team members
options.D: To completely replace the need for physical bedside nursing assessments

explanation: You got it! Technology is there to back you up as a nurse—reducing mistakes and saving time—not to take away your vital human touch.

question: What is the texture of a pureed diet?

options.A: Small, bite-sized pieces of tender meat
options.B: A smooth, pudding-like paste with no lumps
options.C: A mixture of solid chunks and thin liquids
options.D: Crispy foods that dissolve easily in the mouth

explanation: Pureed diets require zero chewing because all foods are blended completely smooth. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T002#GNS227_U6_T002_h3)

question: What is a major problem when a hospital is run using fear and intimidation?

options.A: Staff members tend to hide errors and near-misses out of self-protection.
options.B: The hospital saves money on incident report paperwork.
options.C: Nurses become eager to report every small documentation typo.
options.D: Patient recovery times drop drastically across the board.

explanation: When people are terrified of punishment, they sweep mistakes under the rug—which means the team loses a chance to learn and keep future patients safe.

question: Why must patients finish their full course of TB drugs even after they start feeling better?

options.A: The body needs time to rebuild depleted stomach lining cells
options.B: Health authorities require written proof of finishing all pills
options.C: Stopping early causes immediate permanent liver failure
options.D: Remaining bacteria can multiply and cause drug-resistant relapse

explanation: Feeling better doesn't mean all germs are gone. The toughest ones are still hiding and will bounce back stronger if treatment stops early.

question: Why is a good referral system so important in primary health care?

options.A: It reduces the total number of people visiting government hospitals
options.B: It prevents primary health workers from ever seeing sick patients
options.C: It allows community volunteers to perform major surgeries
options.D: It ensures patients with severe complications get advanced care quickly

explanation: Spot on! A smooth referral system bridges the gap between small clinics and big hospitals, making sure sick patients get the advanced help they need without delay.

question: You look at a medication order and the dose looks unsafe. What should you do?

options.A: Withhold the drug and contact the prescriber to clarify the order
options.B: Administer the medication anyway since the doctor holds the liability
options.C: Change the dose independently based on personal experience
options.D: Ask another patient to take the extra dose to avoid waste

explanation: Never guess or blindly follow a suspicious order! You have a legal duty to protect your patient, so always pause, hold the drug, and check with the doctor first.

question: During early planning, why is open brainstorming without immediate criticism so helpful?

options.A: It encourages team members to share many creative ideas freely
options.B: It ensures that the first suggestion given is always the best one
options.C: It prevents nurses from talking about clinical errors openly
options.D: It speeds up the final approval process by hospital management

explanation: When people aren't afraid of being judged, they feel safe throwing out creative and fun solutions. No idea is a bad idea during brainstorming!

question: What triggers the extrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade?

options.A: The rapid destruction of red blood cells in the spleen
options.B: Direct contact of blood with exposed collagen inside a vessel
options.C: Tissue factor released from damaged outside tissues
options.D: An increase in white blood cell counts during an infection

explanation: The extrinsic pathway is set in motion quickly when tissue factor leaks from injured cells outside the blood vessel. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T3#GNS111_U2_T3_h3)

question: When getting informed consent from a patient for a research study, which of these actions is completely unacceptable?

options.A: Threatening to withhold routine nursing care if the patient refuses to join
options.B: Explaining both the potential risks and benefits of the study clearly
options.C: Ensuring the patient knows they can withdraw at any time without penalty
options.D: Allowing adequate time for the patient to ask questions about the project

explanation: Research participation must always be 100% voluntary. You can never use basic patient care as a weapon or a tool for coercion!

question: What is the nurse's main role when a patient wants to use alternative therapies?

options.A: Forbidding the use of any treatment not taught in medical school
options.B: Ignoring the patient's personal beliefs to focus only on drugs
options.C: Coordinating care safely while respecting patient preferences
options.D: Personally performing every alternative therapy session

explanation: Nurses bridge the gap! We respect what matters to the patient while making sure their overall treatment plan stays safe and effective.

question: What is the main reason why many pregnant women experience constipation?

options.A: Drinking water causes the bowels to become blocked
options.B: Prenatal vitamins stop the liver from producing bile
options.C: High levels of progesterone slow down movement through the digestive tract
options.D: The baby takes up all the space in the stomach and intestines

explanation: Pregnancy hormones relax the body's muscles, including the gut. This means digestion slows down a bit, which is totally normal!

question: Which brain structure acts as the main relay station for sorting incoming sensory information?

options.A: Hypothalamus
options.B: Thalamus
options.C: Medulla oblongata
options.D: Cerebellum

explanation: The thalamus filters and relays sensory signals up to the correct regions of the cerebral cortex. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T3#GNS211_U3_T3_h4)

question: When we talk about 'food availability' in healthcare and nutrition, what does it mainly mean?

options.A: The physical presence of food in a specific area
options.B: The personal preference for certain foods
options.C: The ability of a person to cook a meal
options.D: The amount of money a government saves

explanation: Food availability simply means that food is physically there in the community—whether through local farming, imports, or stored supplies. You've got this!

question: In which layer of the uterus does uterine cancer most commonly start?

options.A: Myometrium
options.B: Perimetrium
options.C: Cervical stroma
options.D: Endometrium

explanation: Spot on! The endometrium is the inner lining of the uterus, and that is where most uterine cancers begin. Keep up the great work!

question: Where is compact bone tissue found in the highest amounts?

options.A: Inside the ends of short bones
options.B: Surrounding the bone marrow cavity loosely
options.C: In the shafts of long bones
options.D: Within the center of flat skull bones

explanation: The shafts of long bones need thick compact bone to bear body weight and resist bending forces. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T2#GNS121_U3_T2_h1)

question: How can a nurse show cultural humility when facing traditional family hierarchies?

options.A: Ignore the patient entirely and speak only to the community leader
options.B: Respect local traditions while still creating a safe space for individual patient input
options.C: Insist that patients completely abandon their cultural beliefs upon entering the hospital
options.D: Follow the hierarchical demands without ever asking the patient their opinion

explanation: Spot on! Cultural humility means respecting culture while making sure the individual patient still has a strong voice in their care.

question: Which main hormone does the body release during prolonged stress to keep your energy up?

options.A: Estrogen
options.B: Thyroxine
options.C: Insulin
options.D: Cortisol

explanation: Cortisol is often called the stress hormone. When stress sticks around for a while, cortisol steps in to keep your energy levels steady. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T15#GNS123_U3_T15_h2)

question: What does syndromic surveillance primarily track during a health emergency?

options.A: Only confirmed laboratory cases of rare tropical diseases
options.B: Hospital staff attendance records during a night shift
options.C: Groups of symptoms before laboratory tests are confirmed
options.D: The exact financial cost of medical equipment used

explanation: Syndromic surveillance watches symptom patterns early on, allowing teams to act fast without waiting for slow lab test results. [learn more](GNS315_U5_T2#GNS315_U5_T2_h4)

question: How should you position an adult patient's ear before using a tympanic thermometer?

options.A: Rotate it clockwise three times
options.B: Pull straight down and forward
options.C: Press it flat against the side of the head
options.D: Pull gently up and back

explanation: Pulling the adult pinna up and back straightens out the curved ear canal so the thermometer has a straight shot at the eardrum.

question: Two clinical supervisors watch the same nursing student perform a procedure and grade them using the same checklist. What are they checking?

options.A: Test-retest validity
options.B: Content consistency
options.C: Inter-rater reliability
options.D: Patient satisfaction

explanation: Inter-rater reliability checks whether different observers get similar scores when using the exact same tool. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T21#GNS224_U1_T21_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of agricultural subsidies provided by the government?

options.A: To lower production risks and support farmers
options.B: To replace natural rainfall with artificial irrigation everywhere
options.C: To increase the retail price of basic food items
options.D: To punish farmers who grow traditional local crops

explanation: Subsidies help farmers manage financial and environmental risks so they can keep producing food reliably. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T028#GNS227_U2_T028_h3)

question: A community health nurse conducts a household survey to count active tuberculosis cases. What type of data is this primarily?

options.A: Hypothetical data
options.B: Quantitative data
options.C: Secondary data
options.D: Qualitative data

explanation: Counting active cases involves numerical measurements, which classifies the information as quantitative data. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h2)

question: Why is a fever in a neutropenic patient treated so aggressively?

options.A: It means the cancer has spread to the skin
options.B: They lack enough white blood cells to fight off hidden infections, leading to rapid sepsis
options.C: Chemotherapy drugs stop working completely if a fever develops
options.D: Fever automatically causes permanent brain damage within minutes

explanation: Without neutrophils, a minor infection can quickly overwhelm the body and cause fatal septic shock, requiring instant antibiotic therapy. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T13#GNS321_U1_T13_h4)

question: Why should you avoid sticking your fingers blindly into a choking patient's mouth to clear an airway?

options.A: They interfere with heart rhythm monitors
options.B: They always cause permanent bleeding of the gums
options.C: They can push the object further down the throat
options.D: They make the patient vomit large amounts of blood

explanation: Blind finger sweeps are dangerous because you might accidentally jam a loose object deeper into the windpipe. Only clear what you can actually see!

question: How does the World Health Organization (WHO) define a safe injection?

options.A: One that does not harm the recipient, provider, or community
options.B: One that uses only glass syringes and metal needles
options.C: One that is administered exclusively by registered nurses
options.D: One that costs less than standard oral medications

explanation: Think of the WHO definition as a circle of safety: it covers the patient getting the drug, the nurse giving it, and the public handling the waste.

question: How do nurses use the idea of homeostatic imbalance when caring for patients?

options.A: To cure infections without using antibiotics by encouraging the patient to rest
options.B: To reverse genetic mutations that caused cellular metaplasia years ago
options.C: To connect abnormal vital signs and lab results to failing physiological control loops
options.D: To prevent the aging process from slowing down organ system functions

explanation: Spot on! When a patient's vital signs are out of whack, a good nurse sees it as a sign that the body's balancing loops are struggling and need help.

question: What is the main difference between managing a healthcare facility and running a regular business?

options.A: Balancing financial viability with clinical outcomes
options.B: Maximizing shareholder dividends above all else
options.C: Focusing exclusively on building maintenance
options.D: Eliminating the need for nursing staff entirely

explanation: Unlike normal commercial businesses, healthcare managers always have to balance the cost of running the hospital with giving the best possible care to patients. You're doing great!

question: What is the primary focus of Management by Objectives (MBO) in healthcare?

options.A: Focusing solely on reducing the hospital's financial budget
options.B: Punishing staff members who miss their daily duties
options.C: Setting specific goals jointly between managers and staff
options.D: Leaving all operational decisions entirely to upper management

explanation: MBO is built on collaboration where leadership and team members agree upon targets together. [learn more](GST321_U2_T5#GST321_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why do DRF programs love buying drugs by their generic names?

options.A: Patients refuse to take medications with brand names
options.B: Generic drugs do not require any regulatory inspection
options.C: Generic drugs are much cheaper than branded equivalents
options.D: Generic medications never expire on hospital pharmacy shelves

explanation: Generic drugs give us the same medical power as expensive brand names, but at a much lower cost—helping keep healthcare affordable for everyone.

question: Which of these is NOT allowed when conducting ethical nursing research?

options.A: Forcing patients to participate to get a large sample size
options.B: Protecting the privacy and confidentiality of patients
options.C: Ensuring participants are protected from physical harm
options.D: Obtaining informed consent from every participant

explanation: Participation in research must always be totally voluntary. Patients should never feel pressured or forced to join!

question: Which nursing action is best for keeping track of a patient's ongoing nutrition?

options.A: Prescribing high-protein dietary supplements independently
options.B: Measuring indirect calorimetry on every single shift
options.C: Calculating precise basal metabolic rate without a formula
options.D: Recording daily weights and monitoring food intake

explanation: Never underestimate the basics! Daily weight checks and watching how much food actually gets eaten give nurses the best clues on nutritional health.

question: What is the main difference between hospital nursing and community nursing?

options.A: Hospital care focuses on acute cure, while community care focuses on prevention
options.B: Hospital care deals exclusively with healthy populations
options.C: Hospital care avoids technology, while community care uses advanced surgery
options.D: Community care only treats patients admitted to intensive care units

explanation: You nailed it. Hospitals treat sudden, severe illness, while community nursing is all about stopping sickness before it starts and keeping people well.

question: A clinical instructor grades a student differently today just because they are in a bad mood. Which core principle is broken here?

options.A: Validity
options.B: Usability
options.C: Objectivity
options.D: Comprehensiveness

explanation: Objectivity means grading fairly based on facts, not personal feelings or moods. Nobody likes a grumpy marker!

question: Which of the following is a direct benefit of electronic health records during shift change handovers?

options.A: Longer meetings that review every patient's childhood history
options.B: Clearer and more complete patient information sharing
options.C: Reduced need for nurses to monitor vital signs
options.D: The complete removal of verbal communication

explanation: Electronic records provide standardized, up-to-date documentation that makes shift handovers much more reliable and efficient. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T1#GNS113_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why is a low salt diet frequently prescribed in clinical practice?

options.A: To prevent sudden drops in blood sugar
options.B: To stimulate a faster metabolic rate
options.C: To reduce strain on the heart and blood vessels
options.D: To increase the body's overall fluid retention

explanation: Excess salt causes water retention which raises blood pressure, so restricting salt lightens the workload on the cardiovascular system. [learn more](GNS227_U6_T007#GNS227_U6_T007_h1)

question: Why might a woman get a positive home pregnancy test even if she is not actually carrying a healthy pregnancy?

options.A: Normal stress levels can trick the urine test strip into changing colors
options.B: Expired test kits always show two lines regardless of hormone levels
options.C: Drinking too much water before the test changes the chemical pH balance
options.D: Certain rare tumors or abnormal tissue growths can also produce hCG hormone

explanation: Because rare conditions can also pump out hCG, lab tests remain categorized as probable signs rather than absolute positive signs. Brilliant clinical thinking!

question: What common fungal mouth infection often pops up when an HIV patient's immune system drops?

options.A: Oral candidiasis (thrush)
options.B: Salivary gland stones
options.C: Gingival hyperplasia
options.D: Dental caries

explanation: Oral candidiasis (thrush) loves to appear in the mouth when immune defenses are low. Easy spot!

question: A patient complains of chest pain and trouble swallowing because their food pipe is squeezing in an uncoordinated way. What is this called?

options.A: Oesophageal varices
options.B: Hiatus hernia
options.C: Oesophageal spasm
options.D: Mallory-Weiss tear

explanation: Correct! When the muscles of the oesophagus contract in a chaotic, painful squeeze rather than smooth waves, it's called an oesophageal spasm.

question: What usually happens when healthcare workers communicate poorly after a mistake?

options.A: Patients recover much faster from their physical injuries
options.B: Families feel ignored and are more likely to seek legal action
options.C: The hospital administration praises the staff for protecting privacy
options.D: Insurance companies automatically pay out large claims

explanation: When we act defensively or fail to communicate well, families feel disrespected. Out of frustration, they are much more likely to take legal action.

question: What is the most common and versatile suturing technique used for simple emergency lacerations?

options.A: Retention bridge stitch
options.B: Simple interrupted suture
options.C: Subcuticular continuous stitch
options.D: Continuous running lock

explanation: Simple interrupted stitches are quick to place and provide reliable closure where each stitch stands alone. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h5)

question: When should a primary health nurse initiate an upward referral for a psychiatric client?

options.A: As soon as the client's symptoms begin to improve on standard medication
options.B: Whenever the client misses a single routine clinic appointment
options.C: When the client develops severe psychosis or active suicidal ideation beyond local management
options.D: When the local clinic runs out of printed health education leaflets

explanation: If a patient's condition becomes too severe for the local clinic to safely handle—like active suicidal thoughts—it's time for an upward referral to specialists.

question: A nurse needs to verify a complex intravenous drug dose quickly before administration. What is the best way to use mobile technology here?

options.A: Use a verified clinical app on a smartphone to double-check the calculation
options.B: Guess the dosage based on how big the patient looks
options.C: Skip the medication entirely if it looks complicated
options.D: Ask another patient in the ward what dose they received

explanation: Mobile reference tools help nurses confirm safe medication dosages instantly at the point of care. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T1#GNS113_U3_T1_h3)

question: During a DRF financial audit, which of these documents is least likely to be checked?

options.A: Pharmacy stock ledgers and count sheets
options.B: Bank statements and deposit slips
options.C: Patient clinical diagnosis charts
options.D: Supplier invoices and purchase orders

explanation: You got it! Financial audits look at money, receipts, and stock numbers—not clinical diagnosis notes, which deal with patient treatment rather than accounting.

question: Why is watching closely for signs of infection so important for patients on chemotherapy?

options.A: Patients are unable to take oral fluids during chemotherapy treatment
options.B: Surgery automatically destroys the lymphatic system permanently
options.C: Chemotherapy lowers the white blood cell count, making the body vulnerable to pathogens
options.D: Ovarian tumors produce bacteria that multiply rapidly in the bloodstream

explanation: Brilliant! Chemotherapy temporarily slows down bone marrow function, leaving the patient with fewer white blood cells to fight off germs.

question: As a caring nurse, why should you check in on the emotional wellbeing of a patient with endometriosis?

options.A: Chronic pain and potential fertility challenges can cause significant emotional distress
options.B: Hormonal medications prevent patients from feeling any physical pain
options.C: Mental health counseling can cure the physical growth of endometrial tissue
options.D: Anxiety and depression are the direct physical causes of retrograde menstruation

explanation: Living day in and day out with stubborn pain and worries about having kids can take a heavy emotional toll. Holistic nursing means supporting her mind too!

question: A nurse needs to draw medication from a multidose vial for another patient. Which of these actions is unsafe?

options.A: Swabbing the rubber top of the vial with an alcohol wipe before piercing
options.B: Using a brand new, sterile syringe and needle for drawing up the dose
options.C: Checking the expiration date printed on the label of the vial
options.D: Leaving a previously used dispensing needle inserted in the vial rubber septum

explanation: Never leave a needle stuck inside a multidose vial! It acts like an open door for bacteria to crawl inside and contaminate the medicine for the next patient.

question: What is the main downside when a nurse suffers from 'under-delegation' (refusing to delegate tasks)?

options.A: Excessive free time for nursing assistants on the ward
options.B: Burnout and exhaustion from trying to perform all tasks personally
options.C: Immediate legal prosecution for negligence by the hospital board
options.D: Complete elimination of patient care errors in the facility

explanation: Trying to do everything yourself on a shift is a fast track to burnout. Trust your team and share the load!

question: Why is risk pooling so important for making healthcare affordable?

options.A: It ensures that sick individuals do not bear the full financial burden alone
options.B: It allows hospitals to buy medical equipment without paying taxes
options.C: It guarantees that doctors receive higher salaries every year
options.D: It stops insurance companies from hiring administrative staff

explanation: Spot on! Spreading financial risk across a big group makes healthcare costs manageable instead of wiping out a single patient's savings.

question: You are putting AED pads on a man with a very hairy chest, and the pads won't stick well. What should you do right away?

options.A: Press the pads down firmly over the thick hair anyway
options.B: Skip using the AED and rely entirely on chest compressions
options.C: Apply conductive ultrasound gel over the dry hair first
options.D: Shave the hair quickly using a razor from the AED kit

explanation: Hair creates air pockets that block the electrical current. Luckily, AED kits come with a handy little razor so you can do a quick dry shave and get a solid stick!

question: During a home visit, you notice the weights for a patient's skin traction are resting on the floor. What is your very first action?

options.A: Document that the patient is non-compliant with bedrest orders
options.B: Remove the traction setup entirely because it is no longer effective
options.C: Ensure the weights hang freely without touching the floor or bed
options.D: Add extra weight to make up for the time the weights spent resting

explanation: Traction weights must always hang free! If they touch the floor, the pulling force stops, and the bones won't stay aligned.

question: A student practices passing a urinary catheter three times on a dummy before doing it on a real patient. What is this called?

options.A: Intrinsic motivational grading
options.B: Passive cognitive observation
options.C: Pedagogical dependency
options.D: Deliberate practice and skill repetition

explanation: Repeating a skill in a safe practice space builds your muscle memory and boosts your confidence for real clinical work.

question: Which condition often develops later if obsessive-compulsive neurosis is left untreated?

options.A: Antisocial personality disorder
options.B: Schizoaffective disorder
options.C: Major depressive disorder
options.D: Dissociative identity disorder

explanation: You got it! Dealing with constant anxiety and exhaustion day after day often leads to clinical depression down the line.

question: What is a common term for spinal nerve root compression caused by a herniated disc?

options.A: Encephalitis
options.B: Neuritis
options.C: Meningitis
options.D: Radiculopathy

explanation: Radiculopathy refers to pain, numbness, or weakness resulting from irritation or compression of a spinal nerve root. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T26#GNS211_U3_T26_h9)

question: Why do we bundle maternal and neonatal health services together?

options.A: Midwives only work during the first week after delivery
options.B: It is cheaper for hospitals to buy medications in bulk
options.C: Newborns require the exact same medical treatments as adults
options.D: The health and survival of the mother and baby are directly linked

explanation: Spot on! Mum and baby are a team. Treating them together ensures nothing gets missed during these crucial early stages.

question: What does the horizontal axis, or X-axis, typically display on a healthcare bar chart?

options.A: The numerical frequency or percentage
options.B: The financial cost of hospital supplies
options.C: The distinct categories being compared
options.D: The exact date and time of a study

explanation: The X-axis holds the group labels, such as different hospital wards or types of procedures. [learn more](GNS217_U4_T7#GNS217_U4_T7_h2)

question: Why should community health nurses plan health programs *with* the people rather than just *for* them?

options.A: It guarantees that government funding will double instantly
options.B: It completely removes the need to write nursing reports
options.C: It ensures programs respect local culture and gain community support
options.D: It allows the nurse to skip doing fieldwork entirely

explanation: Great thinking! When community members are involved from the start, they trust the process more and the program actually fits their daily lives.

question: Why do public health educators emphasize hand hygiene and washing vegetables?

options.A: To stop bacteria from causing secondary cyst infections
options.B: To eliminate adult tapeworms living in human intestines
options.C: To remove lingering agricultural pesticides from produce
options.D: To prevent the accidental ingestion of microscopic parasite eggs

explanation: Good washing habits wash away those tiny dog-shed eggs before they can enter our mouths.

question: A doctor prescribes a proton pump inhibitor to a patient with a stomach ulcer. What is the goal of this medicine?

options.A: Reduced stomach acid production to promote ulcer healing
options.B: Increased release of bile to speed up fat digestion
options.C: Stimulation of the vagus nerve to increase appetite
options.D: Enhanced production of mucus by goblet cells

explanation: By shutting down those acid pumps, the stomach environment becomes less acidic, giving the sore tissue a chance to rest and heal up nicely. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T12#GNS121_U1_T12_h7)

question: When checking if an unresponsive patient is breathing normally, what is the maximum time a nurse should spend on this?

options.A: One minute
options.B: Thirty seconds
options.C: Ten seconds
options.D: Two minutes

explanation: Nice and quick! We check for breathing and a pulse at the same time, but we never want to waste precious seconds—keep it under 10 seconds so compressions aren't delayed.

question: Besides cancer, what other health problem are cytotoxic drugs often used to treat?

options.A: Acute vitamin deficiencies
options.B: Severe autoimmune disorders
options.C: Degenerative bone diseases
options.D: Bacterial respiratory infections

explanation: Correct! Because they calm down overactive cells, these drugs are also helpful for conditions like severe arthritis or lupus.

question: Why is it helpful for a nurse to know the virulence of a germ?

options.A: It shows how quickly the hospital laboratory can bill the patient.
options.B: It helps predict how severe the tissue damage and symptoms might be.
options.C: It dictates the patient's visiting hours in the hospital ward.
options.D: It determines the exact room temperature the patient needs.

explanation: Virulence tells us how strong or nasty a germ is. Knowing this helps you anticipate how sick your patient could get so you can plan better care.

question: How can a clinic best handle scheduling barriers for teenagers who are still in school?

options.A: By refusing service to anyone under eighteen years old
options.B: By forcing students to drop out of school to attend clinics
options.C: By closing down clinics entirely during exam weeks
options.D: By offering flexible operating hours and weekend services

explanation: Flexibility is key! Offering weekend or after-school hours ensures students don't have to choose between their education and their health.

question: Which specific bacterium causes cholera?

options.A: Staphylococcus aureus
options.B: Salmonella typhi
options.C: Vibrio cholerae
options.D: Escherichia coli

explanation: Great recall! Cholera is caused by *Vibrio cholerae*, a bacterium that loves to hitch a ride in contaminated water and food supplies.

question: How is a 'confirmed' case different from a 'suspected' case?

options.A: A confirmed case requires no medical isolation, unlike a suspected case
options.B: A suspected case means the patient has fully recovered from the illness
options.C: A suspected case is always more severe and infectious than a confirmed case
options.D: A confirmed case has laboratory proof of the pathogen, while a suspected case only has symptoms

explanation: Spot on! Lab results turn a 'suspected' case (based only on signs and symptoms) into a 'confirmed' case.

question: What do we call it when a nurse dumps way too many duties onto assistants, making safe care impossible?

options.A: Over-delegation
options.B: Reverse supervision
options.C: Clinical autonomy
options.D: Under-delegation

explanation: Over-delegation happens when team members are stretched too thin beyond safe limits. Balance is key in ward management.

question: Roughly what percentage of a healthy adult human body is made up of water?
explanation: Water makes up about 60% of an adult's weight! That is why keeping hydrated is so vital for every single body function.

question: Why is getting the family involved so important when helping a teen recover from digital addiction?

options.A: Household routines, communication styles, and boundaries heavily influence recovery
options.B: Parents are legally required to operate the patient's smartphone for them
options.C: It prevents the teenager from ever leaving the family home again
options.D: Family members are the only people allowed to prescribe counseling medication

explanation: Healing doesn't happen in a vacuum. Since home life shapes daily habits, the whole family working together makes a massive difference in recovery.

question: What is the main job of sensory receptors in our special senses?

options.A: Pump blood through the sensory organs
options.B: Convert environmental stimuli into electrical signals
options.C: Store memories of past sensory experiences
options.D: Produce hormones to regulate body temperature

explanation: Think of sensory receptors as tiny translators! They take physical things from the world around us—like light or sound—and change them into electrical signals that our nervous system can easily read and understand.

question: Why is it so important to keep interruptions in chest compressions to a bare minimum when using an AED?

options.A: The AED machine will shut down if compressions continue too long
options.B: Stopping compressions lowers blood flow to the brain and heart
options.C: Pausing compressions causes the AED pads to lose their sticky adhesive
options.D: Continuous motion prevents the AED from detecting breathing sounds

explanation: Every second you pause compressions, blood pressure drops and the brain loses vital oxygen. Keep your hands on the chest as much as possible!

question: Why do we need a multi-sectoral approach (involving health, legal, and community groups) to eliminate FGM in Nigeria?

options.A: Foreign donors refuse to fund local healthcare workers
options.B: Federal laws ban NGOs from working in rural areas
options.C: Traditional rulers want total control over all medical and school policies
options.D: No single strategy alone can tackle such deep-rooted social and legal barriers

explanation: Brilliant! Because FGM touches on culture, law, health, and social norms, lasting change requires a teamwork approach across laws, healthcare, and local communities.

question: Why shouldn't nurses just give anti-malarials immediately to every patient with a fever without testing first?

options.A: RDT kits never work during the rainy season
options.B: Patients refuse to take medications without laboratory proof
options.C: Malaria drugs are too expensive to give out freely
options.D: Many other infections can cause similar symptoms to malaria

explanation: You got it! Illnesses like typhoid or UTIs can also cause fever. Testing first stops us from mistreating patients and wasting precious drugs.

question: What is a major risk of trusting pulse oximetry all by itself during a respiratory check?

options.A: Oxygen readings change too slowly to be useful
options.B: Oxygen levels can look fine while carbon dioxide is dangerously high
options.C: Pulse oximeters cannot measure heart rate accurately
options.D: High oxygen readings mean the patient is completely cured

explanation: A great oxygen saturation score doesn't mean they are blowing off carbon dioxide well. Always look at the whole patient!

question: Why are fat-soluble vitamin supplements more likely to cause toxicity than water-soluble ones?

options.A: They are much stronger chemically than water-soluble vitamins and minerals.
options.B: The human liver cannot break them down into less harmful waste products.
options.C: They are stored in body fat and the liver instead of being flushed out in urine.
options.D: They directly destroy the mucosal lining of the stomach when swallowed.

explanation: Because your body holds onto fat-soluble vitamins instead of washing them away, taking too many supplements over time lets them build up to dangerous levels. Moderation is key!

question: What does a positively skewed distribution tell us about patient recovery times?

options.A: The data contains an equal number of fast and slow recoveries
options.B: Most patients take a long time to recover, with very few fast recoveries
options.C: All patients recover in the exact same number of days
options.D: Most patients recover quickly, but a few take a very long time

explanation: Spot on! A positive skew means most people recover fast (piled up at the start), but a few stubborn cases drag the tail out toward longer recovery times.
